articles.title_zh: DealBook Summit: Elon Musk Paints Himself as Political Moderate, Says He Is ‘Not MAGA’
articles.content_orig:
By continuing to use our site, you agree to our Privacy Policy and Terms of Use .
Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post via Getty Images
The billionaire’s comments came during an interview at the New York Times DealBook summit.
Elon Musk, who spent nearly half a billion dollars on Republican campaigns in the recent U.S. midterm elections, is now claiming he is “not MAGA” after a historic blue wave secured Democratic majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives.
“I’m not MAGA,” the Tesla and SpaceX CEO told attendees of the New York Times DealBook summit on Wednesday in a video interview with journalist Andrew Ross Sorkin.
The remark came after Sorkin pressed Musk, speaking remotely from the AMEC Summit in China, over public comments and posts he has made about the issue of immigration. A July Guardian analysis found that the near-trillionaire made twice as many X posts on the subject race and immigration ahead of SpaceX’s initial public offering than he did about his company.
“I’m not sure what MAGA means,” he continued. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party, then I certainly don’t have that. I think there are positives and negatives in both parties.”
The claim marks an about-face for a man who has campaigned with President Donald Trump, worn MAGA hats, and openly called himself “dark gothic MAGA.” Musk was not just the largest individual donor in the 2026 election cycle but across all of U.S. history, according to the Washington Post .
Throughout the conversation, Musk attempted to paint himself as having a more moderate political agenda, saying that he believes D.C. trifectas are dangerous, and claiming that his actual goal was securing a narrow Republican majority in the Senate.
“I think I’m ideologically quite moderate,” he said, adding, “I don’t think I have any kind of extreme political views.”
Elsewhere in the interview, Musk expressed buyer’s remorse over his massive political spending in the 2026 cycle, saying, “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it.”
“Probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money,” he added.
Musk’s $446 million spending in the 2026 cycle came atop more than $240 million spent on Republican campaigns in the 2024 presidential election. In both cycles, GOP advertising frequently deployed anti-LGBTQ+ and specifically anti-transgender rhetoric in an attempt to turn out voters. That strategy proved far more successful electorally in 2024 than it did in 2026. Overall, Republicans spent an estimated $183 million on anti-trans advertising in the midterms ahead of widespread losses.
As the New York Times reported, Musk’s America PAC specifically focused in September on the issue of trans participation in sports to try to defeat Democratic Senate candidates James Talarico, Sherrod Brown, and Josh Turek, who were campaigning in Texas, Ohio, and Iowa, respectively. Talarico, Brown, and Turek all won their races.

articles.title_orig: Was China Sending a Musical Message to Japan’s Takaichi During APEC Welcome?
articles.title_zh: Was China Sending a Musical Message to Japan’s Takaichi During APEC Welcome?
articles.content_orig:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy
I n a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping , is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit , meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.
All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.
“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”
Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.
Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.
The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”
China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”
The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.
The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”
For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”
For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

articles.content_orig:
Follow the latest on Thursday, 19th November, below:
The United Kingdom's Prince Harry said on Thursday he would rejoin the military to fight against Russia if needed.
"If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel," he said in an interview from Ukraine with The Telegraph.
"I think there's a lot that the whole world can learn from Ukraine," the prince said during an unannounced visit to the western city of Lviv over the weekend.
Prince Harry, a former British Army officer and the younger son of King Charles III, traveled to Ukraine for his fourth visit since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, where he met with wounded veterans and medical staff.
"Just because there's not drones, bullets, and rockets flying at us, that doesn't mean that we're not at war," he told the UK newspaper.
He emphasized that "Ukraine are winning" and "there is no version where Russia is making any more advances"
Crimea's Russian-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov said traffic was set to be restored on the attacked Kerch bridge starting from around 4 p.m. local time (1300 GMT) on Thursday.
TASS news agency reported it may take a few months for some sections of the bridge to become operational, citing Deputy ​Prime Minister Marat ⁠Khusnullin.
The bridge, which supports a four-lane roadway and a railroad, is the only bridge linking mainland Russia with occupied Crimea.
Read DW's full report on the most recent Ukrainian attack on Kerch bridge .
The Crimean Bridge was attacked for a third time this week, a Russian official said on Thursday.
Traffic had been temporarily suspended, according to Crimea's Russian-installed governor.
"The damage is currently being assessed," Sergei Aksyonov, the governor, said on Telegram, adding that emergency services were at the scene.
The bridge, which supports a four-lane roadway and a railroad, is the only bridge linking mainland Russia with occupied Crimea.
Read the full article here.
The UK pledged to provide Ukraine with long-range cruise missiles capable of reaching areas in Russia beyond the front lines.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to make that announcement at the "Coalition of the Willing" summit in Berlin.
The drones are a part of the support package for Kyiv worth £260 million pounds ($338 million, €311 million) ahead of the winter.
"Plunging millions of Ukrainians into the freezing cold and starving them of heat and warmth won’t see Putin win this war, it will only cement our resolve to support Ukraine," Burnham said, adding that he is "determined" to help Ukraine defend itself.
According to Burnham, Ukraine's backers are "as united as ever" to secure an end to the war with Russia.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said the meeting of Ukraine's backers in Berlin should send a signal to Russia.
"It's really about time to be serious with the negotiations," Wadephul told DW.
According to Germany's top diplomat, Ukraine's allies are readying themselves for all possibilities, including the failure of negotiations , which would require supporting Kyiv's energy and food needs.
"We will also be on Ukraine's side militarily," he said.
Germany's capital will host a meeting between a group of European leaders that support Ukraine in the war against Russia .
The meeting, dubbed the "Coalition of the Willing," includes German Chancellor Friedrich Merz , French President Emmanuel Macron , British Prime Minister Andy Burnham , Polish Prime Minister Donald ‌Tusk and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will also be in attendance.
According to German officials, the meeting is intended to demonstrate the countries' commitment to legally binding security guarantees should a ceasefire agreement be reached between Russia and Ukraine.
The timing of the meeting is intended to allow the group to react quickly to announcements that come out of the meeting between US President Donald Trump ,Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping in China.
Trump might also meet Putin for a bilateral summit.
Here's more about what's at stake for Europe.
We'll be following updates from the so-called "Coalition of the Willing" meeting in Berlin.
The coalition is a grouping of countries that provide support to Ukraine against Russian aggression.
Leaders of Germany, France, Britain, Poland and Italy, as well as NATO head Mark Rutte, will attend the meeting today.
The show of support comes as Europe tries to forge a unified front in its attempt to be included in the US-led talks to end the war .
We'll have more from Germany's capital, thank you for joining.

articles.content_orig:
Kremlin says Ukraine was the main topic at the Trump-Putin bilateral
U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping pose for a photo during a bilateral meeting in Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. © Reuters
SHENZHEN -- Chinese President Xi Jinping is hosting leaders including U.S. counterpart Donald Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin at this year's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, showcasing his own country's technological prowess against a backdrop of cold and hot conflicts.
The proceedings in the southern tech hub of Shenzhen kicked off with a CEO Summit of business leaders on Tuesday, to be followed by an Economic Leaders' Meeting beginning Wednesday. On the sidelines, Xi and Trump are expected to have their third summit of the year as they seek to manage a fraught superpower rivalry.
As the Ukraine war drags on and tensions with Iran simmer, all eyes are on a trilateral summit among Xi, Trump and Putin that the White House has said will happen on Thursday. This prospect has drawn comparisons to the Yalta conference among the U.S., U.K. and Soviet Union to discuss the fate of postwar Europe in 1945.
Before departing for Asia on Monday, Trump told reporters that he might meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China, a surprise announcement that could become another focal point of his visit.
Nikkei Asia is on the ground in Shenzhen to cover the meetings.

Here are the latest developments (Shenzhen time):
2:57 p.m. The Trump-Xi bilateral summit has ended, CCTV says.
2:49 p.m. Meanwhile, Taiwan's defence ministry said that two Russian military Tu-95 aircraft flew to the island's east on Thursday after approaching from the south, and then exited to its northeast.
2:10 p.m. The Kremlin said the issue of Ukraine was the main topic at the Trump-Putin bilateral, Reuters reported, citing Russia's Tass news agency.
Trump had said that he plans discuss ending the Ukraine war with Xi, and later with Xi and Putin in the bilateral.
2:06 p.m. Xi described China-U.S. relations as overall stable and improving and added he was willing to work with Trump to continue steering bilateral ties on the correct course.
"I remain committed to working with you," Xi said to Trump.
Trump also said he planned to discuss ending Ukraine war with Xi and Putin in the trilateral.
1:58 p.m. Trump said at the start of his bilateral meeting with Xi that the U.S.-China Board of Trade has brought balance to the relationship between the two countries and that they have split up tariffs in fair ways.
Trump added that he and Xi felt strongly that oil should flow through the Strait of Hormuz, where an Iranian blockade in response to U.S.-Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic has restricted shipments and pushed up energy prices. The U.S. president said he will ask China to do more for American farmers, staunch supporters of the Republican party.
1:40 p.m. Trump and Xi pose in front of U.S. and Chinese flags for photos
1:30 p.m. Trump has arrived at the Kylin Villa, a lakeside resort in Shenzhen that will serve as the venue for his bilateral summit with Xi and the trilateral including Putin.
12:43 p.m. Trump met with Putin on the sidelines of the APEC forum following the plenary leaders session. Their meeting comes ahead a bilateral between Trump and Xi and a trilateral among the three leaders.
"We've had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they'll come out of this," Trump told Putin.
1:30 p.m. Trump has arrived at the Kylin Villa, a lakeside resort in Shenzhen that will serve as the venue for his bilateral summit with Xi and the trilateral including Putin.
12:35 p.m. Elon Musk told an APEC organizer that he was a "super fan" of China, according to a social media post by Yuyuan Tiantian, an account affiliated with Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
According to the post, the Tesla and SpaceX boss told Ren Hongbin, president of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, about his admiration for China's "magnificent buildings and natural landscapes" as well as its railway system.
Tesla will continue to increase production in China, Musk said, according to the post. He was photographed sitting in a room across Ren, wearing a black jacket, pants and shoes.
12:06 p.m. APEC plenary session ends
10:58 a.m. Putin tells his APEC counterparts that Russia contributes to regional energy security and that they can "always count on Moscow." He also invites all regional partners to use Russian logistics infrastructure.
10:39 a.m. Trump spoke about the U.S. economy and claimed his administration is taming inflation. He also said in his remarks that trade deals were forthcoming.
"The United States has been a Pacific power for hundreds of years, and we continue to work to promote growth and stability, sovereignty, prosperity, and peace throughout this region," he said.
Trump also said AI regulation needed to be carefully managed and opposed measures that would "stifle" the industry. "We won't allow that to happen," he said.
Trump said he looked forward to meeting with Xi and Putin later this afternoon. but did not elaborate. The trilateral will follow a two-way meeting between Xi and Trump, their third this year.
10:30 a.m. Putin is taking the opportunity presented by APEC to shore up ties with Asian partners. He and Vietnamese leader To Lam agreed to step up cooperation with "a focus on traditional and new energy, including nuclear power, wind power and gas-fired power," according to Vietnam's readout.
The statement also says they "underscored the importance of maintaining peace, security and stability, increasing dialogue and cooperation, and upholding the role of multilateralism, the United Nations and the fundamental principles of international law."
10:10 a.m. In his opening address, Xi called for cooperation on Al and supply chains. The Chinese president proposed building "four key pillars" for development in the Asia-Pacific: economy and trade, connectivity, innovation and development.
He said China will provide $20 million to support cooperation in areas such as digital technology and clean energy.
9:50 a.m. Xi has opened the leaders summit, with the visiting dignitaries gathered around circular tables in a large conference room under chandeliers. Moments before sitting down for the plenary session, they took a photo with Xi in the center, flanked by Putin and Trump. Takaichi was positioned in the back row to the side.
9:40 a.m. In an interview with Fox News, Trump said he spoke with Xi about artificial intelligence, and former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang only came up "briefly," Reuters reports.
"I haven't heard that she was a spy," Trump said, in reference to Huang's extramarital affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang.
9:30 a.m. APEC leaders are gathering for the forum's main event, which begins with a "family photo" before they convene for the plenary session. Xi has urged his guests to pursue "concrete results" promoting economic openness and innovation, but time is limited. Attention in the afternoon will turn to the U.S.-China bilateral meeting and the highly anticipated Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral. There are reports that Trump will squeeze in a one-on-one meeting with Putin as well, although it is unclear how substantial that would be.

articles.title_orig: AI giant Anthropic valued at up to $1.5tn ahead of stock market debut
articles.title_zh: AI giant Anthropic valued at up to $1.5tn ahead of stock market debut
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic has seen its value jump to as much as $1.5tn (£1.14tn) as its shares are set to start trading on the stock market on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said its shares will be priced at $83 each when it lists on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.
That will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.
Anthropic's stock market debut will make it the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public. It will also mark a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which faces questions over whether the huge amounts of money being poured into the technology will be profitable.
The firm said earlier this month it would offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.
But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.
The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.
If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.
Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world's most highly valued stock debut when it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.
However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX shares fell significantly in price .
As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.
The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceX raised in June .
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year.
Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products. Its scope is different from tech giants like Google and Microsoft that also develop AI but are involved in other tech services.
There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.
Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.
"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.
While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.
"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.
Anthropic was started by a group of co-founders , led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.
The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind.
It refused to comply with a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way.
CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present a threat to human existence.
The company has urged developers to slow the development of AI, arguing that advanced systems could pose "catastrophic" risks to humanity if they are not handled with appropriate safeguards.
Rival firm OpenAI has also voiced similar concerns about the technology's risks and delayed its plans to list on the stock market to address AI safety concerns.
Nonetheless, Anthropic is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so.
Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.
"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."
But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent on controversial data centres and funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.
The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.
A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".
With additional reporting by Rachel Clun

articles.title_zh: Mideast nations ramp up efforts to avert all-out war as Israel urges Iran strikes, officials say
articles.content_orig:

The US has carried out further strikes on Iran despite Donald Trump ’s claim that the war is “effectively over” following his humiliating defeat in the midterm elections.
A fighter ⁠aircraft ‌targeted a missile launch site ‌on Qeshm ‌Island after Iran previously struck American personnel and assets in Bahrain, Reuters reported, citing US officials.
Tehran on Wednesday retaliated to US strikes on Qeshm by launching air attacks on Bahrain and Kuwait, the defence ministries of the two Arab nations said. It was Iran’s third strike on American military targets in Bahrain in five days.
Bahrain issued two alerts on Wednesday, urging residents to move to the nearest safe location, before announcing an all-clear after each warning.
It accused Iran ⁠of maintaining a "systematic hostile approach" of targeting the country, which hosts the US navy's Fifth Fleet.
Kuwait said its air defences were countering hostile drone attacks early on Wednesday, without ​providing further details.
Later in the morning, the Iranian army confirmed that it had targeted American drone and missile installations ⁠at ​Kuwait's ⁠Ali Al Salem ⁠base.
The attacks and counterattacks interrupted a roughly two-month lull in fighting and came just days after the US president declared the conflict “effectively over” and played down concerns that he would escalate after the elections.
Mr Trump had signalled Washington would hold off on ordering fresh strikes on Iran, provided there were no new attacks from Tehran or Yemen’s Houthi rebels .
“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters at the White House .
A US official told the Associated Press that Washington used “precision munitions” to strike Qeshm Island in response to the “aggression” towards US personnel. Mr Trump, who is in the Philippines for the Asean summit, told reporters: “We are doing very well in Iran.”
The US carried out limited strikes on Qeshm earlier ⁠this month. Asked for comment, the US military’s Central Command said it had no updates.
Despite the fresh escalation, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said on Wednesday he did not think there was any imminent threat to the US capital, dismissing a CNN report on the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack involving a so-called dirty bomb in Washington.
Mr Trump said the US was ​taking seriously ⁠the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack, while Iran’s foreign ministry denied the “baseless” allegations.
"I am ⁠not," Mr Rubio said when asked if he was concerned about ​an "imminent ⁠attack" on Washington. "I don't think there is ‌any imminent threat."
Mr Rubio added that the US government was "always on the lookout for anything that's a threat to the safety and security of the United States”.
Diplomatic efforts to end the war and open the Strait of Hormuz have been at a standstill despite the efforts of mediators from Pakistan and Qatar.
But Qatari and Iranian officials were meeting on Tuesday, Qatar said, as part of efforts to mediate an end to the nearly nine months of war that have destabilised the Middle East and pushed up global energy prices.
On Sunday, Tehran launched drone attacks on a US military base in Bahrain , following a similar strike on Friday.
Earlier this week, the US deployed a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt , to the Middle East, signalling a potential resumption of hostilities.
The American midterm election results proved devastating for the Republican Party, as voters expressed anger over soaring prices sparked by the unpopular conflict, which was prompted by joint US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran on 28 February.
The US president said officials were taking seriously the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack involving a so-called dirty bomb in Washington, after being asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said the report was part of a US campaign “to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs” using “baseless allegations”.
Trump has also said he will maintain a US naval blockade on Iran because it has continued to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, which is a sticking point in negotiations.
Attacks on tankers have increased this month in the strait, and the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the crew of a tanker passing through the waterway was unaccounted for after being attacked north of the Omani port city of Khasab.

articles.title_orig: Musk says he felt 'pretty foolish' about scale of midterm spending after Republican rout
articles.title_zh: Musk says he felt 'pretty foolish' about scale of midterm spending after Republican rout
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.
The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive was the election's top individual donor , giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.
The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.
Musk was speaking virtually at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
This marks a major shift in tone by Musk, who has previously been seen wearing a Maga hat.
"I'm not just Maga, I'm dark, gothic Maga," he joked at a Trump rally in 2024.
For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.
In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.
Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.
In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings , as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.
Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.
One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According to BBC analysis , Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.
Musk said on Wednesday that he believes Texas' new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, is "going to be quite moderate".
Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, ending more than three decades of the party's control of the state.
The Tesla boss added : "I don't think she's a far-left governor. And based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."

articles.title_orig: Stock Market News, November 18, 2026: Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors’ Nerves
articles.title_zh: Stock Market News, November 18, 2026: Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors’ Nerves
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia’s leadership sought to set a path forward on Tuesday’s earnings call in the wake of former CEO Jensen Huang’s departure — defying calls to re-hire him, reassuring investors that demand for Nvidia’s products remains strong, and indicating that the leadership shakeup could prompt a new or more cautious approach to key elements of the company’s business.
The company has been rocked by scandal, national security concerns and the resignation of Huang, its founder and CEO of 33 years. And leadership was under pressure to reassure nervous investors Tuesday evening, with Nvidia having lost $751 billion in market value since last Sunday.
Many lingering questions remain. But investors appeared at least somewhat mollified by the comments and earnings results: shares ticked up nearly 5% in after-hours trading following the call.
Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang’s return as CEO, tells investors ‘we’ve got this’
Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones kicked off the earnings call by saying the board does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO, despite Huang’s statement earlier Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return should the board allow it.
Jones said the board has “every confidence” in CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress to lead the company as it searches for a permanent replacement. He added the board wants to install a permanent CEO “as quickly as possible,” but it wouldn’t rush to appoint someone until it finds “exactly the right person.”
The board is considering internal and external candidates for the role. And while Jones offered no further hints on who is under consideration, Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing, joined Kress to take analyst questions on the call — a signal of his importance as a senior leader at the company.
Jones indicated that the board is taking the national security concerns into consideration in its search.
“The board appreciates that we’re living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace,” Jones said. “Our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully.”
Why crisis at NVIDIA reverberates across the AI industry
Nvidia has played a key role in fueling the growth of the AI ecosystem by providing financing and investment to its customers to purchase its chips and build AI infrastructure.
Some industry analysts have questioned whether that will continue without Huang, who was considered the industry’s master dealmaker, even as others criticized the practice as “circular financing” that has artificially inflated the market.
Kress said on the call that the company has committed more than $100 billion to such deals as of the end of the quarter ended in October. However, she indicated that the company will carefully evaluate any deals to back would-be customers going forward.
“We remain thoughtful in how we participate and disciplined in how we commit capital,” Kress said. “We are proud of the role that we have played so far in supporting the ecosystem. As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”
Beyond its existing deals, Nvidia will take “a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing,” she said.
The company earned $2.4 billion in sales of licensed chips to China during the third quarter — comprising just over 2% of the total revenue in its core data center business unit. But the company has ceased shipments to the country, Kress said during Tuesday’s call.
That news comes as the company faces increased scrutiny from US officials over the potential illicit transfer of its chips to China.
How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
A complex network of loopholes of shell corporations and unauthorized brokers, often operating via countries like Singapore, are believed to have enabled the transfer of millions of Nvidia chips to China in violation of export controls. Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., estimated that China and Hong Kong “could comprise roughly 15%” of Nvidia’s previous revenues “when considering potential loopholes throughout Asia.”
The Commerce Department on Monday announced tighter export restrictions to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips via data centers in third-party countries.
The company is assuming no revenue from sales of licensed chips to China in the fourth quarter.
Even prior to Huang’s exit, questions were swirling about whether major tech companies might pull back on their spending on AI infrastructure as they face scrutiny from investors over when the technology will produce meaningful returns.
But Kress said demand for Nvidia’s products continues to outstrip supply, especially as a growing slate of companies and consumers seek to implement computing-intensive AI agents .
“Even in the last week, the continued ask is: How are we going to receive more and more supply to help (customers) with the demand that they have in front of them,” Kress said.
That growing demand pushed the company’s projection for full-year revenue growth in 2028 to 75%, up from its earlier projection of 70%. Nvidia also reported better-than-expected guidance for sales in the final quarter of this year.
“We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners,” following Huang’s resignation, Kress said. “They’re all 100% behind us.”

articles.title_orig: What the Crimean bridge attack means for Russia
articles.title_zh: What the Crimean bridge attack means for Russia
articles.content_orig:
It had been a year and a half since Ukraine last attacked the 19-kilometer-long Kerch Bridge connecting Russian-annexed Crimea with Russia's Krasnodar region.
Now, Ukraine has struck again. The attack during the night of November 17 caused the highway section of the bridge to collapse into the sea. As a result, shipping traffic between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov has also been disrupted.
Russia's ministry of transport announced a "temporary suspension" of road and rail traffic on the bridge, though later, rail services were resumed. Russian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into what they are calling a "terrorist attack." It was only after this announcement that the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) confirmed the attack.
The Kerch Strait bridge is considered one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prestigious projects. Its construction began after Russia's 2014 annexation of the Ukrainian Crimea peninsula , an act considered illegal under international law. The Kerch Bridge was completed four years later.
It has been targeted by Ukraine on several occasions since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion . The most well-known strike occurred in October 2022, when an explosives-laden truck detonated on the bridge, causing extensive damage and several months of traffic restrictions. The most recent attack took place in June 2025, when the SBU reported that an underwater support structure was blown up.
The latest Ukrainian operation lasted about a month, and consisted of seven distinct phases. "First, the SBU and armed forces systematically neutralized the enemy's air defense system. After that, the direct attack on the bridge began," says the SBU Telegram channel.
Some Russian military bloggers claim that the attack was carried out with the support of Ukraine's Western allies, or at least using their equipment and weapons.
Ukraine has not confirmed this. It has instead pointed out that various Ukrainian-made weapons were used in the attack, ranging from a variety of drones, to FP-5 Flamingo and R-360 Neptun missiles. British daily The Times has cited Ukrainian military sources, saying that Ukraine attacked the bridge without the support of SpaceX's satellite network system Starlink . There has been no confirmation of this so far.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , meanwhile, described the strike as a response to Russian attacks: "Russia is attacking our infrastructure every day, particularly bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region." He said "we are rebuilding our infrastructure, but we also remind Russia that the war always returns to where it began."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
After the attack, pictures and videos of the bridge were shared on social media. The Krimskij Veter Telegram channel has highlighted damage to the railroad link and questioned why Russian authorities have opted to resume train services.
The Kerch Strait shipping channel is also completely blocked by debris. "This brings road traffic to a standstill, but also shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov," the channel writes.
Indeed, the Kerch Strait navigational channel is merely 120 meters wide, writes Mychajlo Hontschar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" on Facebook. "The strait is shallow, only three to five meters deep."
As early as the 19th century, the seabed was dredged to allow heavier ships to pass from the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov and vice versa. "Now, Vladimir Putin's bridge-building efforts have brought shipping to an indefinite standstill," Hontschar said.
Not only will river-sea vessels no longer be able to leave the waters of the Sea of Azov, the Don, and the Volga, but boats and small ships from the Black Sea fleet and the Caspian flotilla based in Novorossiysk will also be unable to do so.
Many pro-Kremlin Telegram channels have been quick to claim that the bridge does not play an important role in the Russian army's logistics or in supplying Crimea.
The Dva Mayora (Two Majors) channel quotes the "Deputy President of the Republic of Crimea," Olga Kurlayeva, who described the bridge as a "purely civilian structure."
Ukrainian military experts interviewed by DW, on the other hand, point to the systematic disruption of Russian logistics. These efforts also included regular attacks on the R-80 highway leading through Russian-occupied territories of the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions.
Russia cannot replace the Kerch Bridge with any other land connection, says Oleksandr Kovalenko, a Ukrainian military expert with the Information Resistance Group that seeks to counter disinformation. He expects the damaged bridge will cause supply problems for the Russian armed forces: "If there is a resource shortage during attacks or in defense, then either the attacks or the defense will fail."
That is why he does not rule out a decline in attacks from occupied Crimea on the rest of Ukraine. "There are many launch pads for kamikaze drones in Crimea — in the Hvardijsk area, at Cape Chauda and in Balaklava," Kovalenko told DW. "From there, many drones are launched toward Odesa, Mykolaiv, and the right bank of the Dnipro River in the Kherson region. They also fly over Crimea en route toward Ukraine. Then there are attacks using Iskander-M ballistic missiles, as well as Zircon and Oniks missiles, guided missiles, and glide bombs. And while they don't originate in Crimea, they are brought over via the Kerch Bridge."
Kovalenko says the bridge strike has dealt a serious blow to Vladimir Putin's standing. It comes at a sensitive time as Putin is about to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Shenzhen, China .
Memes and witty comments about the bridge abound on X. Meanwhile, the Russian president's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has promised to rebuild the bridge and assured that it will be "even better than before."
Andrii Korezkyj of the Kyiv University of Transportation, however, says this is not likely to happen anytime soon. "All in all, I would estimate that it would take between one and a half and three years [to rebuild]," Korezkyj told DW, adding, "I don't think they'll let the Russians build another [bridge] arch like that near the Ukrainian border without interference."
Pro-Russian commentators, known as Z-bloggers, agree with this view. "Unlike in 2022 and 2023, the Ukrainian armed forces are now able to launch strikes against floating cranes and repair teams."
"Even installing a pre-assembled arch under these conditions would constitute a challenging task," writes the pro-Kremlin Rybar Telegram channel.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title_orig: Xi Jinping rallies against protectionism as he welcomes Trump to Apec summit
articles.title_zh: Xi Jinping rallies against protectionism as he welcomes Trump to Apec summit
articles.content_orig:
Chinese president greets US counterpart with rare hug before blockbuster trilateral meeting with Putin
China’s Xi Jinping rallied Asia-Pacific nations against trade protectionism on Wednesday morning before heading to the airport to welcome Donald Trump , whose administration has just further restricted advanced chip exports, with a rare hug.
The Chinese president spent Wednesday’s opening day of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit switching lanes between multilateralist and big-power politics, culminating in a group photo where he stood central among fellow leaders. He was flanked by Trump and Vladimir Putin – whose blockbuster trilateral meeting will dominate Thursday’s proceedings as the summit gets to its business end.
Having all delegates in the photograph was a tightrope feat in itself, with potential Canadian and Australian refusals to stand with Putin over the war in Ukraine shelved out of respect for the host.
The Russian president did not arrive in a conciliatory mood, using his speech at the summit to call western powers “former hegemons”, state that Europe was in “a humiliating decline” and proclaim that sanctions no longer worked.
However, toasting his varied visitors at a welcoming banquet, Xi invoked “the grand plan for Asia-Pacific cooperation”. Thursday would see those gathered “discuss measures to expand mutual openness, explore pathways for innovation-driven growth, [and] broaden opportunities for pragmatic cooperation in various fields,” he said.
Openness was the main theme of his keynote address, presenting China as a stalwart of free trade and technological innovation.
“We find ourselves in a changing and turbulent world. Global growth lacks momentum, and unilateralism and protectionism are rampant,” he told the audience of business executives and Apec leaders. “We should firmly safeguard the WTO-centred, rules-based multilateral trading system, support free and open trade and investment, and keep global industrial and supply chains stable and unimpeded.”
Critics of Beijing have long accused it of hypocrisy on this point, noting the obstacles many foreign businesses face entering China’s vast market. But Xi’s messaging on open trade was echoed by other leaders who took to the stage after him, including South Korea’s Lee ⁠Jae Myung and Malaysia’s Anwar Ibrahim.
Putin meanwhile took aim at sanctions, claiming they had “largely run their course, having ⁠lost much of their intimidating power”.
That prompted a rebuttal from Canada’s Mark Carney, who told reporters Putin was “lying”. “Sanctions are very real and they’re going to continue to increase as long as this war goes on,” he said.
When Xi met Putin though, he called for closer political and military ties between Russia and China, in a continued demonstration of a tight relationship that has only deepened since Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Before Putin’s arrival in China, Russia sent nuclear-capable bombers to an airport in Vietnam, in a rare deployment interpreted as a pointed show of Moscow’s ability to project strength in the region despite being embroiled in the Ukraine war. Russian military aircraft had spooked air forces in both Taiwan and Japan on Tuesday as they flew past them while routeing south from Russia’s Far East region.
It was Xi’s reception of Trump, complete with an embrace, that broke with convention; the reception on the airport tarmac is believed to be the first by a Chinese leader in decades, although during Xi’s state visit to Washington in September, Trump had also taken the unusual step of greeting Xi on the tarmac.
Xi travelled to the airport despite the US announcing on Monday new interim rules to further restrict Beijing’s access to advanced semiconductors. That followed an awkward week of news after the chief executive of US chipmaker Nvidia resigned over an affair, reportedly with a woman some US officials suspect of being a Chinese spy.
Beijing’s “overriding objective” was “extending the fragile calm in the US-China relationship for as long as possible”, Ryan Hass, from the Brookings thinktank, told the AFP news agency. “[The reception] set a positive tone for Trump’s visit, marking a contrast from the swirl of news around the Jensen Huang scandal that preceded Trump’s arrival in Shenzhen.”
The state news agency Xinhua said Xi had noted “China is a nation with a tradition of courtesy that values reciprocating goodwill”, after Trump met Xi at the airport when he visited the US.
Trump and Xi will hold a bilateral meeting as well as talks with Putin on Thursday. On Wednesday, the Associated Press reported that Trump had said he and Putin would meet separately as well, citing an anonymous US official.
These meetings will dominate the day’s schedule and the news cycle, a fact that has at times seemed to bother China.
“The Chinese actually tried to have this meeting not happen … They kind of got jammed into it. Then, when it was going to happen, they just wanted statements,” the former US national security adviser Jake Sullivan said on The Rest is Politics podcast. “They are going to be deeply uncomfortable throughout this because this does not fit their narrative of a country that believes in multi-alignment, the United Nations, everyone around the table.”
Shen Weizhong, a former policy planner with China’s foreign ministry who now works for the Global Governance Institution, a Beijing-based thinktank, told the Guardian he would not be surprised if Sullivan was right and that China was “torn”.
“On the one hand, it will steal the spotlight. The outcome is not clear and there are no immediate deliverables,” he said. “But on the other side, it will help China’s image – it is the only facilitator who could do this, and if it can ease tensions on the world stage, that will be good.” He said he suspected enthusiasm from both Putin and Trump for the meeting could have ultimately swayed Beijing.
China is actively opposing the framing of the meetings as a new Yalta , the 1945 meeting between Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt that in effect carved up postwar Europe. “The global south will not like having a Yalta 2.0, and China is always taking the smaller countries into consideration,” said Shen.
Also potentially on Thursday’s agenda is an Apec joint statement that, an official told Reuters, delegates were “working around the clock” to find agreement on. “China as host will want something,” said Shen, though even Beijing is “not as obsessed with such deliverables” these days.

articles.title_orig: Crew unaware of risks before Bayesian yacht accident, say investigators
articles.title_zh: Crew unaware of risks before Bayesian yacht accident, say investigators
articles.content_orig:
The crew of the Bayesian superyacht did not know about a critical safety risk that left it vulnerable in powerful winds before it sank off the coast in northern Sicily coast, killing seven people, British investigators say.
British tech tycoon Mike Lynch, 59, and his daughter Hannah, 18, were among seven people who died when the vessel sank on 19 August 2024 .
The sinking of the Bayesian unfolded with "extraordinary speed" when a violent downburst of freak hurricane-force winds knocked it onto its side in less than 15 seconds, the UK's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) final report said.
Safety information provided to the crew did not identify this type of risk, the MAIB said.
"It was very dynamic, very quick," said MAIB principal inspector Simon Graves. "The speed of events overtook the crew and prevented them from taking any other action."
In addition to Mike Lynch, 59, the accident led to the deaths of his daughter Hannah, 18, Morgan Stanley International bank chairman Jonathan Bloomer, 70, and his wife, Judy, 71.
An American lawyer, Chris Morvillo, 59, and his wife Neda Morvillo, 57, also died, along with crew member Rick Thomas , 59.
Rob Loder, chief inspector of marine accidents said: "Our thoughts remain with the families and loved ones of the seven who lost their lives, and with all those affected by the loss of Bayesian. This accident developed with extraordinary speed."
Fifteen survivors escaped from the 56-metre (184m) luxury yacht and managed to get to a life raft that had been launched by a crew member.
The marine investigation found that the Bayesian "had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down".
In addition, "the extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk", Loder added.
In the early hours of 19 August 2024 the Bayesian was anchored outside of Porticello port, on the north coast of Sicily.
With thunderstorms rapidly coming in, wind speeds went from 8 knots to about 70 knots (80mph) within minutes. The weather forecast had only predicted gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph).
The MAIB report stated that with no sails set Bayesian was vulnerable to being knocked over in severe winds.
A study commissioned by the MAIB indicated that, in the conditions assessed, Bayesian was vulnerable to extreme winds at the vessels widest point, known as the beam.
It also found that any knockdown - where the boat was suddenly tipped sideways - would be "irrecoverable once the yacht passed the angle of vanishing stability", assessed in the study as being 73 degrees. Once the vessel passed this angle it could not right itself.
In addition, the centreboard, which provides stability when a ship is under sail, was raised. The report said the centreboard was not needed when the Bayesian was using its motors and was rarely lowered at anchor. The way the boat was loaded, and the angle of the wind, also contributed to the accident.
Inspectors said a "downburst of hurricane-force winds" was the most likely cause of the ship keeling over.
They happen when cold, dense air plunges rapidly, sending out violent winds across the surface.
The MAIB said that none of risks were covered in the UK training syllabus, nor in published guidance available to crew.
Once the vessel was on its side, it rapidly filled with water and sank.
The MAIB's final report into the sinking, published on Thursday, appeared to contrast with recent reports from Italy, where prosecution experts have reportedly blamed errors by the crew rather than problems with the yacht.
The investigation was carried out alongside a criminal probe in Italy , where captain James Cutfield, chief engineer Tim Parker Eaton and deckhand Matthew Griffith are under investigation over potential charges of multiple manslaughter and culpable shipwreck.
British investigators said that Italian prosecutors had restricted access to some witnesses and evidence.
"It is possible that the circumstances depicted in this report may alter following disclosure of evidence withheld by the Italian authorities," the report says.
However, the MAIB's Graves said he was satisfied with the British investigation.
"We are content with our investigation, the investigation that we've undertaken, and the information we've used to feed into it."
The report also found that alcohol consumption had not contributed to the sinking.
The MAIB report makes seven recommendations to four agencies. It calls for new regulations to be set for single-hulled sailing vessels, and new rules around life rafts.
It also urges collaboration between the Met Office and its global counterpart to improve information-sharing of severe weather forecasts with mariners.
The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is also investigating the sinking.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO live: Company said to price stock at $83, begin trading Thursday
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO live: Company said to price stock at $83, begin trading Thursday
articles.content_orig:
Retail investor Dan Shetty is so eager to get in on the Anthropic initial public offering that he "drained" his Roth IRA and moved roughly $12,000 from Fidelity to Robinhood for a chance to participate.
"I don't want to tell my grandkids that I didn't invest in Anthropic and I didn't invest in OpenAI during the AI bubble," he said.
Shetty's enthusiasm is shared by many, with excitement among small investors for the blockbuster IPO expected to be off the charts. Vanda Research estimates that Anthropic could see approximately $250 million of retail net buying when it starts trading Thursday, double the size of SpaceX's IPO.
"That would be far and away the largest amount of net retail buying of any stock that we've seen in our data on the first day of its listing," Jai Malhi, senior strategist at Vanda, said in an interview with CNBC.
The artificial intelligence laboratory — which will trade on the Nasdaq under ticker symbol ANT — is selling 825 million shares at an expected price range of $70 to $78 per share in the IPO, though sources told CNBC the stock is likely to price above that range . Individual investors are expected to be allocated as much as 20% in that initial offering. And if Vanda's figures prove correct, the buying enthusiasm will be big as regular trading begins.
Founded less than six years ago, Anthropic aims to raise as much as $64.4 billion, giving it a valuation of $1.405 trillion. If demand is especially strong, Anthropic could even raise more than the record $85.7 billion that SpaceX sold in its record IPO in June.
The tech trade has been in turmoil since Jensen Huang's departure last week as Nvidia CEO raised questions about the future of AI financing. Before then, a potential slowdown in data center development resulting from Democratic victories in the 2026 midterm elections, and signs of moderation in the capital expenditures boom, had already spooked investors.
These all stand in marked contrast to the market backdrop in place at the time of the SpaceX IPO. In June, both positioning and sentiment were high, Malhi said. The Anthropic IPO could see a different dynamic, however. Demand could be strong across the entire investor spectrum given that sentiment is depressed, meaning that the bar to beat expectations is "much easier to overcome," he explained.
"What we're seeing across both retail and institutional positioning is that there is plenty of dry powder to take part in this IPO," the strategist said.
For the 27-year-old New Yorker Shetty, who himself works at agentic data platform Data Workers, this is his first time vying to take part in an IPO. He said Anthropic's emphasis on "safety first" drew his interest.
"I've been telling all of my friends, 'If you have like $5, you should invest it in this stock because this is the pure-play AI leader,'" Shetty said. "I think of my father who invested in Microsoft during the dotcom bubble, and he divested from that stock, and it was such a silly thing to do."
Joe Pak, a former macro portfolio manager who is now an independent researcher outside London, is opting against participating in the Anthropic IPO for two reasons: the likelihood of limited allocation and current macroeconomic conditions.
He believes the odds are probably stacked against retail investors when it comes to the allocation of shares.
"It's very difficult as a retail investor to actually get an allocation in these blockbuster IPOs," the 36-year-old said. "You get maybe one share, and the base case is you don't get any at all. So, it's a bit of a catch-22. If you do get a lot of shares, it probably means that the institutional bid was weaker, and in that case, you don't actually want the shares at that level."
In terms of the economy, conditions "need to be favorable" to hold a position in a stock like Anthropic, he said. But with the Federal Reserve having raised interest rates in September and widely expected to do so again next month, the backdrop could be darkening.
"The risk that you have is the financial conditions deteriorating" before the company starts to grow into anticipated profit and revenue, which would justify purchase of the stock, Pak said.
While Pak is steering clear of the IPO, he did say that at a certain level, it would make sense to get into Anthropic.
Other retail investors such as Bryan Nearnberg share Pak's view.
"I'm planning to eventually buy Anthropic, just not at the IPO price, considering when the lockups expire and there's some selling pressure," said the 37-year-old Westchester County, N.Y. resident, who works in finance operations. "We are not at the end of this short-term negative headline sentiment."
IPOs are a sore spot for Nearnberg, who hasn't had much luck trading stocks on their opening day. His skepticism toward IPOs can be traced all the way back to when he was in college.
"I didn't get an allocation to the Facebook IPO, but I ended up buying it the first day of open. I got burned pretty quickly," Nearnberg told CNBC. "Same thing with Zynga. I didn't get an allocation, but [got] burned pretty quickly in terms of price."
As a result of those experiences, "I'm pretty sure we'll see a good entry price underneath the IPO for Anthropic by Memorial Day next year," Nearnberg said, citing sour sentiment toward technology and  concern surrounding circular financing as short-term headwinds.
To be clear, all the retail investors CNBC spoke with are optimistic on AI as a transformative technology — even the ones sitting out the IPO. One trader said he believes in AI so much that he uses Anthropic's Claude, a conversational AI assistant, every day.
But Russ Faigen, a 27-year-old in Austin, Texas, is undecided on whether to subscribe for a piece of the IPO.
"From a price-to-sales ratio, Anthropic's like a really good deal," Faigen said. But "it's still a massive valuation for a $1.4 trillion company, and there are significantly better deals out there if you are a fundamental investor."
Faigen, who works for an agentic brokerage firm, said he's "leaning towards patience," as he believes Anthropic is going to be public "for a very long time."
"I just am not in a rush to get in on day one based off the valuation," he told CNBC.
Anthropic's valuation depends on its ability to sustain its rapid growth. In the nine months through Sept. 30, revenue reached more than $33 billion, 1,200% above the year-earlier period. Aggregate spending commitments total about $900 billion , primarily centered around computing power and infrastructure.
Breakneck growth leads plenty of retail and institutional investors to approach not just the Anthropic IPO but the entire AI trade with caution.
"A lot of it comes down to scrutiny over how much money they're spending on AI," said Bret Kenwell, U.S. investment analyst at eToro. "Investors want to see that those investments are turning into tangible returns, into tangible revenue."
— CNBC's Charlotte Morabito contributed to this report

The artificial intelligence company Anthropic said on Wednesday it sold more than 956 million shares at a price of $83 a piece in a record-breaking initial public offering that makes it one of the most valuable companies in the world.
The five-year-old AI powerhouse raised around $79.4 billion through the offering, exceeding the $75 billion IPO haul of Elon Musk's SpaceX earlier this year. Anthropic's shares will start trading publicly on Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.
The listing was oversubscribed, despite coming at a time of growing concern about a possible AI bubble and volatility in tech stocks.
The number of shares sold and the price exceeded Anthropic's original expectations. The listing prospectus targeted a sale of 825 million shares at $70 to $78 per share.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin Will Sit Down for the First Time. It Won’t Be Like Yalta.
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin Will Sit Down for the First Time. It Won’t Be Like Yalta.
articles.content_orig:
Leaders of the US, China and Russia to take part in their first trilateral, with developments on trade, AI and global conflicts closely watched
Xi Jinping rallies against protectionism as he welcomes Trump to Apec summit
What is Apec? Explained in 30 seconds
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec), taking place today in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.
It’s a big day for global diplomacy, with a hotly anticipated meeting between US president Donald Trump, China’s leader Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin .
It is the first time ever the three leaders have held trilateral talks – with the meeting even drawing comparisons to the 1945 Yalta meeting, shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.
On the agenda is Russia’s war with Ukraine , the US war in Iran , as well as global trade, AI, and nuclear weapons .
Speculation also abounds about the possible appearance of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un , with Trump saying he is open to engagement.
Stay tuned for an exciting day in global affairs.
Along with the coterie of world leaders at Apec , hundreds of business leaders are also in Shenzhen, with executives from BYD, Baidu, Boeing and Google set to attend .
Elon Musk is also expected to be there, along with Visa CEO Ryan ⁠McInerney, Mastercard CEO Michael Miebach and Deloitte CEO Joe Ucuzoglu.
Despite the high-profile roster of names, Nikkei Asia has reported that the number of prominent US executives appears “relatively light” compared to previous years. One official told the publication that executives had not been provided with clear agendas in advance and many were caught up in scheduling conflicts.
One major name present at the event in South Korea last year, but noticeably absent from this year’s summit, is Jensen Huang, who resigned from Nvidia last week after a scandal over an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China.
South China Morning Post reports that the chaos that has engulfed the chipmaker in the last week has played a role in discouraging some US business leaders from attending the summit, as they “worry about being perceived as close to China”.
Zak Dychtwald, the founder of BridgeWorks Global, a China-based consultancy told the paper that “CEOs had spent the last 18 months returning to China with more confidence, and this sets that back”.
Here’s the Guardian’s Rebecca Bailey on Xi Jinping’s speech today, in which she writes that he reiterated themes of openness and innovation emphasised throughout the summit.
“China is an advocate, promoter and forerunner of Asia-Pacific economic cooperation,” he said. He announced China would give US$20 million in funding “to support APEC’s practical cooperation”, and would establish a Apec-focused research centre in Shenzhen.
“Efforts should be made to align various regional economic and trade agreements, boost trade and investment facilitation and digitalisation, and reduce barriers to trade and investment,” he said.
The region should promote connectivity and innovation, he added. Green energy, energy and food security and digital infrastructure were all among areas mentioned for more coordination and collaboration.
Toward the beginning of his speech he had this poetic flourish:
double quotation mark Members of Apec are like passengers riding the same ship. To navigate the waves of the Pacific, we must unite as one and look out for each other.
President Trump has shared some of of his thoughts on AI saying that Apec opposes regulation that would “stifle” the industry.
“We won’t allow that to happen,” he said.
Commenting on concerns about AI, the US president said:
double quotation mark It’s almost completely good, but it’s got some bad elements and we have to be very careful” in managing the bad.
Trump said his meeting on Thursday with Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin was already a “win” before it took place, Reuters news reports.
The unprecedented diplomatic gathering of the leaders of the world’s largest nuclear ⁠powers is unlikely to produce major agreements , analysts ⁠say, while it unnerves smaller countries that ​fear their interests might be disregarded.
Xi greeted Trump at the airport , ⁠the first time he has done so with any visiting leader since becoming president, reciprocating his counterpart’s gesture at Joint Base Andrews in September when they last met. The leaders also briefly hugged.
double quotation mark This is a great president, one of the great presidents of China, and he’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Trump ⁠said, when asked what he wanted to get out of the unprecedented three-way meet.
And not only that, the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people, the young children, the soldiers, the whole thing. ​It was great respect, and I appreciate that. That’s a big win for us. It’s ‌a big win for China too.
Here it is, the Apec family photo !
The gathering, hosted by China’s Xi Jinping , is attended by leaders from the 21-member grouping.
There has been ample speculation that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un may attend Apec , with Trump and US secretary of state saying they are willing to engage.
The Kremlin has also signalled Putin’s willingness to meet in Shenzhen.
In recent days the media has been tracking the elusive North Korean leader to assess his wheareabouts.
But there has been no sign of him in China so far , and photos released in recent days show him busy inspecting a tourism zone in Samjiyon .
And also a construction site in Hamgyong .
Kim’s visit to the construction sites in ‌the eastern province of the country could indicate the North Korean leader did not intend to attend Apec , said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea’s Kyungnam University, Reuters reports.
There is, it seems, plenty at home for him to do.
An update on the alleged global espionage scandal that unfolded in the lead-up to the Apec summit:
US President ⁠Donald Trump said he spoke to ⁠Chinese ⁠President Xi ​Jinping about artificial intelligence , but ⁠reference to former Nvidia CEO ⁠Jensen Huang only came ​up “briefly” ‌in ‌the discussion.
double quotation mark We did ‌not discuss it. I might have referred to it just briefly because ‌it’s such a tragedy. It’s ​a tragedy. He’s such a brilliant man,” Trump said ⁠in an interview ​to ​Fox News ​that was broadcast ​during ‌the network’s “The ​Ingraham ​Angle” show.
Jensen Huang ⁠resigned after revelations about extramarital affairs, including with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed and alleged Chinese spy.
The Guardian’s correspondent Rebecca Bailey is in Shenzhen, where she is covering the events of the day.
Describing the mood on the ground and what we can expect today, she writes:
There’s a sense of anticipation in the air, and traffic restrictions on the road, as we kick off the final day of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit. Today will be a blockbuster day of geopolitics , featuring both multilateral discussions and back-to-back big power negotiations .
Leaders from Apec’s 21 member states will shortly gather for a family photo, before going into a plenary session, according to a White House schedule.
Host Xi Jinping will then meet Donald Trump at a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park in the early afternoon. Just under two hours later Vladimir Putin will join them for unprecedented trilateral talks, according to that schedule. In addition, it has been reported that Trump and Putin might meet separately.
Also potentially on Thursday’s agenda is an Apec joint statement that, an official told Reuters on Tuesday, delegates had been “working around the clock” to find agreement on.
